conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:

2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.

   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text

   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.

    or outcomes.

    conversation is synthetic.

14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with infected breast ulcers and right heel pain. She had recently undergone a breast biopsy, and the wound became infected due to inadequate dressing changes. Cultures grew Pseudomonas, and she was treated with intravenous antibiotics, later transitioned to oral therapy. Imaging showed no abscess or osteomyelitis. Her right heel had a non-infected pressure injury with underlying bone spurs, managed with offloading. She also had symptomatic bladder sludge in the setting of low urine output from ESRD, treated with a short-term catheter and antibiotics. Social work coordinated home care with family support, avoiding rehab placement per patient preference. She remained stable throughout, completed dialysis, and was discharged home on a 14-day antibiotic course with follow-up arranged.

HISTORY:  ___ woman with end-stage renal disease who undergoes
dialysis via left upper extremity graft created in ___.  Graft has
required percutaneous intervention since as early as ___ and as
recently as last month and is currently occluded by physical exam.  Last
dialysis ___.  No bruit on exam.

PROCEDURES:
Contrast study of graft with central venography, pharmacologic and mechanical
thrombolysis, balloon venoplasty and ___ balloon sweeping of graft with
angiographic review after each ste performed via bidirectional ___ access in
each side of graft.

OPERATORS: Dr. ___ (___) and Dr. ___ (attendinG). The
attending paticipated in the entire procedure.

TECHNIQUE:  Prior to the study, the procedure, expectations, risks and
alternatives were discussed with the patient and consent was signed.  In
Interventional Radiology, the patient was placed supine on the table with the
left upper extremity extend out to the side.  The skin over the patient's
palpable graft was prepped and draped in the usual sterile manner after repeat
physical examination.  Preprocedure timeout was performed per ___ protocol. 
Initially, ultrasound examination over the graft was performed and images were
stored.  After infiltration of skin and superficial subcutaneous tissue over
the graft, a micropuncture needle was introduced under direct ultrasonographic
visualization into the graft near the arterial anastomosis directed centrally.
The 0.018 wire for the kit would not pass through the clot and thus exchange
was made for a 0.018 nitinol wire, which was advanced and coiled in the graft
to allow passage of a micropuncture sheath.  After exchange for a 0.035
system, a 0.035 angled Glidewire was used to negotiate through the occluded
graft, and more centrally across the stent into the native venous outflow. 
Micropuncture sheath was exchanged for 4 ___ multihole straight catheter,
which was advanced to the patent vein just beyond the patient's stents and
central venogram was performed and recorded digitally.  Based on the results
of this, exchange was made for a short 6 ___ sheath and with this secured
in place, access into the venous end of the graft was performed in a similar
technique as described previously, but directed towards the arterial
anastomosis.  A 6 ___ short sheath was also placed here.

Via the centrally directed access and then via the arterially directed access,
AngioJet catheter was passed for installation of tissue plasminogen activator
(TPA) for a total dose of 9 mg of TPA within the clotted graft.  This was
allowed to sit for approximately ___ minutes, during which time preparations
were made for AngioJet for thrombolysis.  This was again performed in both
directions and both hand injection and a recorded digital run were performed
to assess progress.  Based on this, balloon maceration of clot was performed
through the length of the graft with repeat imaging after this.  A 4-mm
___ catheter was then carefully advanced over a 0.018 glidewire placed via
the 6 ___ sheath which was directed peripherally.  The Glidewire was
advanced up into the inflow artery, and the balloon was inflated and pulled
back with the wire into the graft and was swept centrally.  Repeat imaging was
performed.  Though at this point, there was a pulse in the graft and some
flow, there was still considerable irregularity and no thrill.  Hand was
examined intermittently. Repeat high-pressure balloon inflation with the 7-mm
balloon was then performed from the stent and graft junction through the
length of the graft.  Repeat imaging showed incomplete improvement and some
residual filling defects in the stents and thus a repeat AngioJet for thrombus
removal was performed without TPA.  At this point, a weak thrill was felt in
the graft.  Based on results of imaging, the arterially directed 6 ___
sheath, (the one close to the venous outflow) was removed and a pursestring
suture applied.  With that sheath out of the way, finally, 8 mm long-term
high-pressure balloon inflation was performed at the stent/graft junction and
at the persistent narrowing of venous end of the graft and a final
angiographic run was recorded.  The final 6 ___ sheath was removed and a
pursestring suture applied.  The hand was examined.  Dry, occlusive sterile
dressings were applied and the patient was sent to the holding area for
recovery.  She was to undergo dialysis on ___, rather than
being sent immediately to dialysis.

A total of 4000 units of heparin were administered intermittently via both
sheaths during the course of this exam, prior to balloon inflation.

FINDINGS:  On arrival, note was made of no pulse or thrill along the patient's
palpable left upper extremity graft.  Initial 0.018 wire would only pass
partially through the thrombosed graft as described above and ultrasound
images showed echogenic material filling the lumen of the graft.  The arterial
anastomosis was visible on ultrasound and a +2 radial pulse was palpable.  (No
ulnar pulse palpable).

Initial hand injection into the graft opacified interstices of clot, but there
appear to be flow beyond the stents.  Central venogram showed no obstruction
along the level of the axillary vein, subclavian vein and down to the level of
the right atrium.  During the course of interventions, there was eventually
flow seen from a widely patent arterial anastomosis into the loop graft, but
restoration of palpable thrill required repeat AngioJet to remove
non-occlusive thrombus in the stent and high-pressure balloon inflation across
persistent irregular narrowing at the stent/graft junction and in the venous
end of the stent very close to our access point.  By the end of our
interventions, there was excellent antegrade flow through the loop graft and a
palpable thrill.  As has been noted before, the patient's graft takeoff is
from one of two duplicated brachial arteries, but these appear smooth and of 4
mm caliber.  Previously placed stents remain well expanded.  Left radial pulse
remained palpable throughout and after the exam and the patient's only
complaint was related to left upper abdominal pain, which had been ongoing and
which she reports is related to sites of insulin injection.

ANESTHESIA:  1% local lidocaine was administered as described and the study
was performed under moderate sedation with continuous hemodynamic monitoring. 
A total of 5 mg of intravenous Versed and 250 mcg of intravenous fentanyl were
administered in divided doses during a total intraservice time of 223 minutes
and this was administered via an independently trained nurse who was not
otherwise participating in the procedure.

Estimated blood loss 35-45 cc with sheath flush/aspiration and AngioJet
suction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in because your dialysis access wasn't working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I couldn't get dialysis today. My arm felt fine, but they said no blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned painful bumps on your abdomen where you inject insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they've been getting bigger for three weeks. I finished antibiotics but no improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you've had burning when you urinate and cloudy, smelly urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for about three weeks. I finished another antibiotic but still feel the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We'll check your arm, abdomen, and urine. You're not running a fever, but we'll start antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I'm worried about my dialysis access failing again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We'll get imaging on your arm tomorrow to see what's going on. For now, rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan shows your bladder wall is inflamed, likely infection. The abdominal bumps aren't abscesses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it's not calciphylaxis again? I couldn't tolerate that treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No calcium deposits were seen. We'll watch them as possible panniculitis. No treatment change now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That's a relief. What about my arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a clot in your AV graft. You'll have a procedure today to clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it work? I've had clots before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiologist is experienced. They'll use medication and tools to open it. Success is likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure was successful. The clot is gone, and blood is flowing through your graft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you! Can I do dialysis tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, scheduled for tomorrow. We'll also check your breast wound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It's been oozing a little. Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We took a sample. It grew E. coli and Proteus, both sensitive to the antibiotic we're giving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? That was painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Different bacteria, but we're treating it effectively. Ultrasound shows no abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my urine infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture was contaminated, so we can't confirm. But your symptoms are improving with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You completed dialysis yesterday. Your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want to finish your IV antibiotics. You'll get them during dialysis sessions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I'll go home and come back for antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the antibiotic will be given after each dialysis. We'll switch to oral if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my wound care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wound care team recommends daily dressing changes with saline and special packing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can do that at home with help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and follow up with your wound nurse practitioner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is down, creatinine improving. You're healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any news on the back spot from the CT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lytic spot in your spine is likely benign, maybe a Schmorl's node. MRI can clarify if needed later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I'd rather not unless it's urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Agreed. We'll monitor. Your blood pressure is stable on your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're doing well. We'll plan discharge tomorrow if labs stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I'm ready to go home. Will I need rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Physical therapy says you can go home with support. We'll arrange services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final labs look good. Your infection markers are down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You'll get ceftazidime after each dialysis for now. Repeat urine culture if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my abdominal bumps?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with dermatology if they change. No treatment now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're cleared to go home. Take your meds, do wound care, and attend dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for fixing my access and treating the infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Call if you develop fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And check labs in a week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and follow up with nephrology and your primary team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. You handled everything well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We'll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I'll make sure to keep all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That's the best way to stay healthy. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Call us with any concerns.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for a thrombosed left upper extremity AV graft, preventing dialysis. She also reported persistent abdominal nodules at insulin injection sites and chronic urinary symptoms. Imaging confirmed bladder wall enhancement suggestive of infection and a non-specific lytic lesion in L1, but no abscesses or calciphylaxis. The AV graft was successfully recanalized via thrombectomy. Wound culture from a prior breast biopsy grew pan-sensitive E. coli and Proteus, treated with targeted IV ceftazidime. Urine culture was contaminated, but symptoms improved with empiric antibiotics. She completed one dialysis session during admission and was transitioned to outpatient IV antibiotic administration post-dialysis. Discharged home with services, on a plan for continued dialysis, wound care, and close follow-up for unresolved abdominal nodules and repeat urine testing if symptoms persist.
